title: Love God, Serve Man -- Ch. 1: Love God, Serve Man
keywords: the poor, the afflicted and the weak
He Profits Most Who Serves Best
Save A Heart, Save A Life
Prayer of St. Francis of Assisi
primary_topics: Chapter 1 of 'Love God, Serve Man' -- CJP's July 12, 1990 induction address as president of the Rotary Club of Manila, in which he announced LOVE GOD, SERVE MAN as the Club's new credo and declared that upon this credo he would be judged not only in Rotary but in his whole unworthy life here on earth.

His three-point VISION for Manila Rotary, structured as a triad and a pyramid: the Club exists for its members, colleagues and guests; for excellence in the professions, business, education and government; and mostly and most importantly for the poor, the afflicted and the weak, which is its base and driving force.

A detailed, budgeted program of action for 1990-1991 -- 67 committees, medico-surgical missions, an eye bank, immunization drives, scholarships, street-children and livelihood projects -- requiring at least P10 million against a past record of P5 million, with dues held flat and P7 million to be raised from other sources.

The theological grounding of Rotary service: Paul Harris' maxims restated as spiritual truth, the thrice-repeated command to Peter to feed My sheep, and the judgment that asks not about bank accounts or diplomas but about feeding the hungry and clothing the naked -- making service to man the best expression of love of God.

Peace as the fruit of social justice rather than the absence of violence, drawing on Jose P. Laurel, the Catholic Church and Pope John Paul I, with Manila Rotary contributing to peace by relentlessly pursuing its credo.
sub_topics: He opens by thanking the Club for installing him as president in its 72nd year, noting that no one runs for president in Manila Rotary -- under an election procedure unique in all of Rotary, the top vote-getter for the board is automatically proclaimed, sometimes contrary to his wishes.

He is humbled by predecessors who included Senate President Gil J. Puyat, Supreme Court Justice George A. Malcolm and the diplomat-soldier-statesman Carlos P. Romulo, and pays special tribute to Jonby Carlos, president 34 years earlier and still active.

He recounts the Club's standing -- the oldest in Asia, the largest outside the United States with 455 members -- quoting his former professor, Justice Edgardo L. Paras, that Manila Rotary is undoubtedly the best civic club on this side of the world.

Elected as early as December 1989, he used seven months to pray about, reflect on and plan his incumbency with his incoming team, producing a printed Program of Action stating goals, describing projects and fixing the dates for their completion.

First point of the VISION: weekly Thursday meetings at the Manila Hotel, a revitalized Balita with a monthly supplement, fellowship and sports activities, energy and water conservation and traffic safety, membership raised from 455 to 500 and attendance from 78 to 83 percent, and cooperation with other clubs and districts.

Second point: excellence promoted through the Rotary 4-way test in city, municipal and barangay centers, journalism awards, vocational and teacher values-formation programs, graduate scholarships and exchange teams abroad, an overseas-employment program, national oratorical and essay contests, a choral festival, support for the Boy Scouts and the Philippine Cancer Society, and a new Search for the Most Outstanding Public Servants.

Third and most important point: six medico-surgical missions for about 4,800 poor patients, free eye operations and an outreach clinic for 10,000 patients plus a new eye bank, a WHO-assisted immunization campaign for 1,000 children, health and nutrition education for 300 families, free heart surgery under Save A Heart, Save A Life, a drug-abuse program endorsed by President Corazon C. Aquino, hearing conservation for 1,000 patients, the Rotary Village Corps in San Andres Bukid, scholarships for 300 Don Bosco students and 50 college grants, the Sagip Kabataan Center, a newsboys' Mini-Olympics, shoeshine stands, a livelihood pilot project, Preserve Planet Earth advocacy, emergency relief, and a re-invigorated Social Justice Committee.

The budget: at least P10 million is needed against a previous high of P5 million, yet the board decided not to increase dues, which will total only P3 million, leaving P7 million to be raised, with Sonny Belmonte and Roger Cabunag spearheading the effort.

The raison d'etre: he vows to channel the Club's treasure, time and talent to the less fortunate, because helping those who cannot help themselves and cannot help us back in return is the reason for being of Manila Rotary.

The warning and the duty: if the rich who are few will not help the poor who are many, the few who are filled cannot escape the wrath of the many who are hungry -- so feeding, clothing, comforting, sheltering and protecting are not an option but a duty of the well-to-do, the talented and the privileged.

The judgment scene: the Creator will not ask how many digits are in our bank accounts or how many diplomas or plaques we hold, but whether we fed the hungry and healed the sick, for as often as you did it for the least of My brothers, you did it for Me.

The theological roots of Rotary: Paul Harris' Service Above Self and He Profits Most Who Serves Best were mouthing not just a capitalist doctrine but a spiritual truth, and LOVE GOD, SERVE MAN is their theological restatement.

The Peter passage: three times the risen Christ asked Simon Peter whether he loved Him and three times commanded him to feed My lambs and feed My sheep, showing that love for God requires tending the flock, particularly the young and the helpless.
The eschatological turn: Rotary service for those who have less in this temporal life can become the key to the gate of eternal life, so Rotary work ceases to be merely for the here and now.

The response to Rotary International: to President Paolo V. C. da Costa's theme HONOR ROTARY WITH FAITH AND ENTHUSIASM and his Preserve Planet Earth call, the Club pledges to honor Rotary by loving God with child-like faith and serving man with contagious enthusiasm.

Peace defined: not the absence of violence, the stalemate of nuclear terror or the silent subservience imposed by dictators, but the fruit of social justice -- giving every man his due, helping him live with dignity -- invoking Justice Jose P. Laurel's humanization of all laws, the Church's solidarity of those who have more with those who have less, and Pope John Paul I on love of God and neighbor.

The close: he reiterates the three-point VISION, names the commitment to the poor the cornerstone of his presidency, submits to be judged upon the credo, and invites everyone to rise and recite the Prayer of St. Francis of Assisi.

notable_anecdotes: The presidency nobody runs for: he notes that he was never a candidate, because under Manila Rotary's election procedure -- unique in the entire world of Rotary -- the top vote-getter for the board is automatically proclaimed president, sometimes even contrary to his wishes.
Leaning on a predecessor: he singles out Jonby Carlos, president 34 years earlier in 1956-57 and still active in the Club, for the privilege of leaning on him for support and counsel.

His professor's verdict: he quotes Justice Edgardo L. Paras, his former professor and a fellow member, that Manila Rotary is not only the first and largest Rotary Club in Asia but undoubtedly the best civic club on this side of the world.

Seven months of preparation: elected in December 1989, he spent the interval in continuous meetings with his incoming team and produced a printed Program of Action distributed to the audience that evening.

The budget gap announced from the rostrum: P10 million needed against a previous high of P5 million, with dues left untouched at P3 million and Sonny Belmonte and Roger Cabunag named to raise the remaining P7 million.

The examination at the end: he pictures standing in utter nakedness before the Creator, who will ask not about bank accounts, diplomas, plaques or even churchgoing, but whether we fed the hungry and sheltered the homeless.
The closing prayer: he asks the whole Fiesta Pavilion to rise and begin the quest for peace by reciting together the Prayer of St. Francis of Assisi.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'Love God, Serve Man' is the address CJP delivered on July 12, 1990 at the Manila Hotel Fiesta Pavilion on his induction as president of the Rotary Club of Manila, where he announced the credo that gives the book its title. He begins with humility and history: he had never been a candidate, since under an election procedure unique in all of Rotary the top vote-getter for the board is automatically proclaimed president; his predecessors included Senate President Gil J. Puyat, Justice George A. Malcolm and Carlos P. Romulo; and the Club, at 455 members, is the oldest in Asia and the largest outside the United States, which he says has loaded a heavy burden upon his lean and unworthy shoulders. Elected as early as December 1989, he spent seven months planning with his team and produced a printed Program of Action built on a three-point VISION, structured like a triad and a pyramid: Manila Rotary is for its members, colleagues and guests; for excellence in the professions, business, education and government; and mostly and most importantly for the poor, the afflicted and the weak. He enumerates the programs under each point -- weekly meetings and membership targets, the 4-way test and journalism and scholarship programs, and a long list of charitable projects from medico-surgical missions and a new eye bank to immunization drives, Save A Heart, Save A Life, Sagip Kabataan, newsboys' Mini-Olympics and shoeshine stands -- and states the budget frankly: P10 million needed against a previous high of P5 million, with dues unchanged and P7 million to be raised. The raison d'etre, he says, is to help those who cannot help themselves and to help those who cannot help us back in return, for if the rich who are few will not help the poor who are many, the few who are filled cannot escape the wrath of the many who are hungry. He then grounds Rotary's maxims theologically in Christ's threefold command to Peter to feed My sheep, defines peace as the fruit of social justice, and closes by submitting to be judged upon the credo and inviting all to recite the Prayer of St. Francis of Assisi.
